interview_log.question_text: Please tell me about yourself. Who are you, in your own words?
interview_log.dj_answer:
Hello, I'm Dong Jae Lee. Career-wise, if I were to summarize my career in one sentence, it would be 'bridging the gap between deep tech and real-world business.' I built my foundation at KAIST, majoring in Mechanical Engineering and Industrial Design. This gave me the literacy to understand complex technology, but my real passion has always been finding the market value within that technology and turning it into a viable, growing business.

My career has been defined by two distinct phases:
First is the 'Zero to One' phase. I co-founded a tech startup called Flint Technologies. As the COO, I experienced the raw reality of building something from nothing. I didn't just strategize; I executed—from defining the MVP and finding Product-Market Fit to securing seed funding and handling investor relations. This experience taught me grit, agility, and how to make critical decisions with limited resources.

Second is the 'Scaling' phase. As the Director at Devs United Games, I focused on global expansion and monetization in the XR space. I led high-stakes partnerships with global platforms like Meta, Apple, and Google.

In short, I offer the best of both worlds: the technical depth to earn the respect of engineering teams, and the business acumen to drive revenue and strategy. I'm looking forward to bringing that versatility to your team.

On a personal level, I am someone who runs toward new challenges, not away from them. My resume reflects a diverse path—from engineering to founding a startup, and then to scaling a gaming business. This isn't because I lack focus, but because I am not afraid of being a beginner again if it means solving a harder, more meaningful problem. I thrive on that steep learning curve.

But no matter where I go, one thing remains constant: my reputation. I take great pride in the fact that my former colleagues—leaders, peers, and engineers alike—are my strongest advocates. They know me as someone who works with an owner's mindset: I don't just 'clock in'; I own the problem until it's solved.

I believe this combination of adaptability and reliability is why people always want to work with me again.

areas_to_improve: Answer runs ~3 minutes — should be under 2 for Altos
Generic phrases ('best of both worlds', 'runs toward challenges') weaken specificity
TmaxTibero experience missing from narrative — important for completeness
Should mention international background (4 countries) more naturally
Mentioned KAIST Mechanical Engineering & Industrial Design — but answer direction suggests KAIST AI MS should be highlighted
interviewer_feedback.follow_up_question: You said you 'secured seed funding and handled investor relations' at Flint. How much did you raise, from whom, and what was the hardest moment in that fundraising process? Give me a number and a story.

follow_up_exchanges.follow_up_question: How much did you raise, from whom, and what was the single hardest moment in that fundraising process?
follow_up_exchanges.dj_answer: Strong Ventures and Fast Ventures invested $212K in our Seed Round at a $2.127M post-money valuation, for a 10% equity stake (preferred stock). Later we secured a KRW 200 million bank loan with a guarantee from KODIT. The hardest moment was convincing VCs to invest on our terms despite two unfavorable conditions: (1) US incorporation — Korean VCs disliked the 해외투자신고 bureaucracy, and we had several meetings where they tried to convince us not to incorporate in the US. (2) Equal 25% equity split among all 4 founders — VCs in Korea don't prefer this structure. We held firm on both because US incorporation was strategically necessary and equal equity was the fair thing to do since all founders were fully committed.

strengths: Specific numbers: $212K, $2.127M post-money, 10% equity, KRW 200M KODIT loan
Named actual investors (Strong Ventures, Fast Ventures)
Showed conviction — pushed back on VCs on two structural issues
areas_to_improve: Could add: why was US incorporation strategically necessary? (one sentence would strengthen)
The 'fair thing to do' framing is honest but could be more strategic in real interview

follow_up_exchanges.follow_up_question: Equal 25% across 4 founders — most VCs push back for a reason. Did it create problems at Flint?
follow_up_exchanges.dj_answer: Pros: everyone had the same weight, same responsibility. No doubts or complaints about shares, which allowed us to focus on work. Cons: decision-making was hard initially — numerous meetings and votes. We tried many methodologies. In the end, as engineers, we decided to trust data. We would find ways to obtain objective data and agreed to follow it. Example: when deciding product direction (generic tool vs specific use case), each founder had different visions. We designed separate UIs and landing pages for each idea, released them publicly, measured reactions over a set time period, then followed the most validated idea. We learned 'disagree but commit' — even if your idea lost, you must not work any less because it wasn't chosen.

strengths: Moved from structural problem to concrete methodology (landing page tests)
'Disagree but commit' principle — maps directly to VC investment committee dynamics
Honest about the cons, not defensive
areas_to_improve: In real interview: explicitly connect this to VC IC process — 'I've already lived the model'
interviewer_feedback.interviewer_note: Strong answer. The equal-equity → data-driven resolution → disagree-but-commit arc is a compelling narrative that demonstrates maturity. Recommended to use this story in actual interview.

overall_observations: DJ speaks confidently and structures answers well
Needs to tighten delivery for Altos's conciseness standard
Should lean more into specific numbers and stories, less into category labels
Bilingual delivery is natural and strong
When pushed for specifics, DJ delivers strong concrete stories (fundraising, equity structure)
The Flint equal-equity → data-driven culture story is interview gold — recommend using proactively
